## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical use of image signing and CI enforcement for early security.

## Key Concepts
- Cosign signing and verification
- Image allowlists and registry trust
- GitHub Actions integration for a gate

## Code Example
```yaml
name: cosign-gate
on:
  push:
  pull_request:
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Install cosign
        run: |
          curl -sSfL https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/download/v1.20.0/cosign-linux-amd64 -o cosign
          chmod +x cosign
          sudo install cosign /usr/local/bin
      - name: Verify images
        run: |
          cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/secure/app:1.2.3
```

- How would you rotate the cosign key in CI?
- How would you extend the gate to handle multiple environments and teams?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design multi-facet security gates across image provenance, container hardening, IAM, and network posture within a Helm-based workflow. It also assesses tooling integration (cosign, Kyverno, OPA) and practical verification.

## Key Concepts
- cosign image signing and repo-backed public keys
- Helm chart security: readOnlyRootFilesystem, runAsNonRoot
- RBAC least-privilege patterns in Kubernetes
- OPA/Kyverno policies for mTLS and egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno policy snippet enforcing readOnlyRootFilesystem and runAsNonRoot
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: enforce-container-security
spec:
  validationFailureActions: enforce
  rules:
  - name: require-security-context
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: [ Deployment, DaemonSet, StatefulSet ]
    validate:
      message: "Containers must run as non-root and with readOnlyRootFilesystem"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              securityContext:
                runAsNonRoot: true
                readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test the CI gate against a large repo with many charts? 
- What trade-offs exist between strict mTLS enforcement and operational flexibility?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests end-to-end security design for multi-cloud Kubernetes workloads, focusing on identity, secret management, and policy enforcement with real-world tools.

## Key Concepts
- Zero-trust workload identity (SPIRE)
- Ephemeral credentials (Vault)
- Service mesh security (Istio, mTLS, AuthorizationPolicies)
- Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego)
- Egress controls to data lake and namespace isolation

## Sample Solution

### 1. SPIRE Workload Identity
```yaml
# spire-workload.yaml
apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterSPIFFEID
metadata:
  name: data-platform-workload
spec:
  names:
    - data-service
    - analytics-service
    - etl-service
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production
```

### 2. Vault Integration for Secrets
```yaml
# vault-secret-store.yaml
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultSecret
metadata:
  name: data-lake-credentials
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  vaultAddress: https://vault.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:8200
  path: secret/data-lake
  provider: hcp
  refreshInterval: 1h
```

### 3. Istio AuthorizationPolicy
```yaml
# istio-authz.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: data-lake-access
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: data-lake-gateway
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["spiffe://data-platform/data-service"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
        paths: ["/v1/tables/*"]
```

### 4. OPA Policy Example
```rego
#.rego
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.namespace == "restricted"
  not input.request.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg = "Pods must run as non-root"
}

allow[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment"
  input.request.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged
  msg = "Privileged containers not allowed"
}
```

### 5. CI Enforcement Check
```yaml
# .github/workflows/security-scan.yml
name: Security Scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  opa-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run OPA policy check
        run: |
          opa eval --fail-defined-deny \
            --data policy.rego \
            --input manifests/
```

## Key Takeaways
- SPIRE provides cryptographically secure workload identity
- Vault enables dynamic secret rotation without application changes
- Istio mTLS ensures service-to-service encryption
- OPA/Rego enforces admission control and runtime policies

## Why This Is Asked
This question probes practical policy design at scale, focusing on admission controls, RBAC hygiene, and network isolation in a multi-cloud Kubernetes environment. It tests how a candidate translates security requirements into Gatekeeper constraints and integrates them into CI.

## Key Concepts
- Open Policy Agent (OPA) Gatekeeper constraint templates
- Kubernetes security: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, privilege constraints
- RBAC hardening: disallow cluster-admin bindings, namespace-label exceptions
- NetworkPolicy defaults and whitelisting
- CI integration: manifest validation, test manifests, failing/passing samples

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate: noPrivileged
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8snopriv
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sNoPriv
  targets:
  - target: AdmissionReview
    rego: |
      package k8snopriv
      violation["privileged container"] {
        input.review.object.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged == true
      }
```

```yaml
# Constraint
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sNoPriv
metadata:
  name: no-privileged-containers
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test these policies locally against a sample manifest?
- How would you manage exceptions for ops-managed namespaces without weakening security?

name: Security gate
on: [push]
jobs:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

          tags: myservice:latest

## Why This Is Asked

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal GitHub Actions workflow (yaml)
name: SBOM and vulnerability gate
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: |
          docker build -t myimage:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock anchore/syft:latest DockerImage:${{ github.sha }} -o json > sbom.json
      - name: Scan with Trivy
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock aquasecurity/trivy:latest image --exit-code 1 --no-progress myimage:${{ github.sha }} || true
      - name: Scan with Grype
        run: |
          grype myimage:${{ github.sha }} -o json > grype.json || true
      - name: Upload SBOMs
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: sboms
          path: sbom.json, grype.json
      - name: Fail if CVEs found
        run: |
          if [ -s grype.json ] && grep -q '"score": 7' grype.json; then exit 1; fi
```

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests foundational secure supply chain practices in a beginner-friendly manner. It mirrors real-world CI gates used in production environments around Dockerfile hygiene, image signing, SBOM generation, and registry controls. It introduces modern tools like Cosign and SBOM attestations without overwhelming complexity.

## Key Concepts

- **Dockerfile Hygiene**: Non-root USER and multi-stage builds reduce security vulnerabilities and image size
- **Container Image Signing**: Using Cosign to sign and verify container images ensures integrity
- **SBOM Attestation**: Software Bill of Materials provides transparency into image contents and dependencies
- **GitHub Actions Workflows**: Implementing gates and policy checks in CI/CD pipelines
- **Registry Allowlist**: Restricting deployments to approved registries prevents supply chain attacks

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow
name: Docker Security Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Validate Dockerfile
        run: |
          # Check for non-root USER
          grep -q 'USER ' Dockerfile || exit 1
          # Check for multi-stage build
          grep -q 'FROM.*AS' Dockerfile || exit 1
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} -o spdx-json > sbom.json
      
      - name: Sign image and SBOM with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
          cosign attest --type spdx-json --predicate sbom.json ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Verify signature and attestation
        run: |
          cosign verify ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
```
